Research and compare suitable artificial-intelligence PhD directions and programs abroad for an application horizon of roughly 1–2 years.

Cover major regions including North America, Europe and Asia. Compare research strengths, curriculum structures, academic resources, employment prospects, application and language requirements, research/internship preparation, tuition, scholarship and funding mechanisms, and representative universities or programs.

Produce a phased 1–2 year preparation and application plan covering research preparation, program selection, application materials and timeline management.

1. Which 1–3 AI problems or research themes most interest you? This will determine which directions, laboratories, prerequisites, and projects the report emphasizes.
2. What is your primary post-PhD objective: academic research, industrial R&D, entrepreneurship, or applied leadership? This will change how programs are weighted for publication culture, internships, industry links, and placement.
3. What is your current AI-PhD readiness profile, including highest degree and field, grades, key math/CS coursework, research or publications, and substantial AI/software experience? This will determine the reach/match shortlist and the gaps addressed in the 1–2 year plan.

1. Natural language processing and deep learning, especially applied, implementation-heavy AI research and system building.
2. Industrial R&D, while preserving strong research and employability options.
3. I am currently a Computer Science and Technology undergraduate at a prestigious university in Jiangsu. My academic performance is excellent, and I have received school scholarships for two consecutive years; my exact GPA is not specified. I mainly prepare through self-directed coding, online learning, technical blogs, and GitHub, using tools such as PyCharm and VS Code extensively. Specific math/CS courses, research experience, publications, and major AI/software projects are not specified.

As of September 13, 2026, which artificial-intelligence PhD research directions and programs abroad would best fit me over a roughly 1–2-year application horizon, given that I am a Computer Science and Technology undergraduate at a prestigious university in Jiangsu, have excellent academic performance and two consecutive years of university scholarships, and am primarily interested in natural language processing and deep learning—especially applied, implementation-heavy research, experimental engineering, and AI system building—with the long-term goal of industrial R&D while retaining strong academic-research and general employability options? Compare major destinations in North America, Europe, and Asia, including differences between direct-entry PhDs from a bachelor’s degree, programs that expect or require a master’s, structured doctoral programs, and professor- or project-based positions. First, identify and compare promising NLP/deep-learning subfields—such as language-model training and adaptation, efficient and scalable ML systems, retrieval and knowledge-intensive NLP, multimodal language systems, evaluation and reliability, human-centered or domain-applied NLP, and other relevant emerging directions—without assuming that I am committed to any narrower topic; assess each direction’s research maturity, prerequisite knowledge, implementation intensity, publication opportunities, compute and data requirements, fit with industrial R&D, likely durability beyond current trends, and representative laboratories, faculty, papers, and employers. Then compare representative universities and programs across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, continental Europe, Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, and other justified destinations, evaluating faculty and laboratory fit, recent research strengths and output, curriculum and qualifying-exam structure, degree duration, supervision model, access to compute/data and interdisciplinary centers, industry collaborations and internships, publication culture, alumni placement, local AI employment prospects, post-study work or immigration considerations, and practical risks such as dependence on a single supervisor or grant. For each representative program, summarize official eligibility and application requirements for an international applicant educated in China, including whether direct bachelor-to-PhD admission is possible, expected academic and mathematical/CS preparation, English-language tests and waiver rules, GRE or other testing policies, research-proposal requirements, faculty-contact norms, deadlines for likely 2027 and 2028 entry cycles where published, application fees, tuition, mandatory charges, estimated living costs, stipend levels, funding duration, teaching or research obligations, scholarship mechanisms, and whether funding is guaranteed, competitive, supervisor-dependent, or insufficient for normal living expenses. Clearly distinguish official facts from estimates and compare costs in local currency plus a common reference currency when feasible. Produce a region-by-region comparison and a provisional reach/match/safer shortlist or tiering methodology, while explicitly noting that my exact GPA, class rank, university name, core mathematics and CS coursework, research experience, publications, major AI/software projects, English proficiency, preferred countries, budget, and personal constraints have not been specified; do not invent these facts, and explain how different values would change the recommendations. Include a diagnostic checklist for those missing details and identify the highest-priority readiness gaps likely to matter for NLP/deep-learning PhD admission. Finally, create two concrete preparation pathways—an accelerated approximately 12-month route and a stronger approximately 18–24-month route—with month- or quarter-level milestones for auditing prerequisites in linear algebra, calculus, probability/statistics, optimization, algorithms, systems, machine learning, deep learning, and NLP; reproducing influential papers; building technically substantial and reproducible GitHub projects; obtaining research-assistant experience and mentorship; choosing feasible research questions; conducting experiments and writing a paper or technical report; targeting suitable conferences, workshops, or preprints without encouraging low-quality publication; pursuing relevant industrial or research internships; preparing English tests and any required standardized tests; developing a faculty/program tracking system; contacting potential supervisors appropriately; securing strong recommendation letters; drafting the CV, statement of purpose, research statement/proposal, and writing sample; selecting balanced application portfolios; and managing deadlines, interviews, offers, funding comparisons, and contingencies such as applying first to a research-oriented master’s or full-time research-assistant position. Prioritize primary and current sources: official university, department, graduate-school, funding, immigration, and faculty/laboratory pages; original papers and official proceedings from venues such as ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, and relevant systems conferences; and official employer or government labor information. Link directly to those sources, state the access or update date, flag information that may change by the application cycle, and use secondary rankings or blogs only as clearly labeled supplementary context rather than decisive evidence.

The student seeks an artificial-intelligence doctorate abroad within a roughly one-to-two-year application horizon and favors natural language processing and deep learning, especially applied, implementation-heavy experimental engineering and AI system building, with a long-term goal of industrial research and development while preserving strong academic and broad employment options. Compare promising directions without assuming a narrow prior commitment: language-model pretraining, post-training, adaptation, alignment and agents; efficient and scalable machine-learning and language-model systems; retrieval-augmented generation, search, knowledge-intensive natural language processing and data-centric methods; multimodal language systems; evaluation, robustness, interpretability, safety and reliability; human-centered natural language processing; low-resource, multilingual, speech-language, embodied, scientific, biomedical, legal, financial and other domain-applied natural language processing; and justified emerging directions. Cite representative current laboratories and faculty across North America, Europe and Asia, seminal and recent original papers or official proceedings in ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR and relevant systems venues, and representative employers. Prioritize primary sources and direct links, mark access/update dates, distinguish sourced facts from analytical judgments, and avoid reliance on rankings. Return dense, structured material suitable for a final advisory report.

Cover the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, continental Europe (include several of Switzerland, Germany, Netherlands, France and Scandinavia as justified), Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, and any additional destination justified by unusually good fit. ## **List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

**Research date/context:** September 13, 2026.

### 1. Broad proceedings search for major AI/NLP research directions

**Tool:** `web_search`  
**Query:**  
> `site:aclanthology.org OR site:proceedings.neurips.cc OR site:proceedings.mlr.press large language models pretraining RLHF RAG scaling laws multimodal evaluation robustness multilingual seminal paper`

**Maximum results requested:** 10  
**Search engine reported:** `ddgs_brave_fallback`

**Results returned:**

1. “A Survey of Post-Training Scaling in Large Language Models” — ACL Anthology PDF. Search-result note: “Open this URL with web_fetch before using it as evidence.” [1]
2. “Aligning Large Multimodal Models with Factually ...” — ACL Findings 2024 PDF. Search-result note: “Open this URL with web_fetch before using it as evidence.” [2]

I need official/original sources spanning Transformer/pretraining/scaling, post-training/alignment, retrieval, efficient systems, multimodal, evaluation/safety, and representative faculty. Next I should search specifically for primary landmark papers and systems venues, then a separate search for current lab/faculty pages.”

## **Fully Comprehensive Findings**

### A. Scope actually covered by the completed research

The completed searches identified candidate sources in the following areas:

- Large-language-model post-training and post-training scaling [1]
- Factual alignment of large multimodal models [2]
- Language-model scaling laws [3]
- Multimodal supervised fine-tuning scaling laws [4]

### B. Primary-source candidates surfaced

The proceedings-oriented search surfaced the following apparent primary or official publication records:

The researcher concluded that the first search “surfaced useful recent primary papers but not the foundational set or labs/programs.” The second search supplied direct arXiv pages for BERT and RETRO, but the researcher judged that “search quality is weak for the broader primary-source set” and that several sources still needed to be verified by opening them.

### C. Secondary reading-list and discovery sources surfaced

The foundational-paper search also returned several secondary resources:

- “Foundational AI/ML papers — the canonical reading list.” [11]

- “Top 35 Research Papers in Large Language Models - LLMBase.” [20]

These were surfaced as discovery aids. No page was opened, and no claims from these resources were verified. The researcher explicitly judged the broader search quality as weak and preferred “stable known official proceedings/direct paper links.”

### D. Laboratories and university research organizations surfaced

The laboratory/faculty search returned the following official university pages:

- MIT CSAIL Natural Language Processing Group [21]
- Berkeley NLP Group [22]

It also returned two secondary discovery resources:

The researcher’s assessment was:

> “Official US group pages are found, but the query underrepresents Europe and Asia.”

The researcher also stated that current affiliations must be checked carefully:

> “I need representative—not exhaustive—current faculty across all three regions, and must avoid stale affiliations.”

No individual faculty names, current supervision availability, current institutional affiliations, admission policies, or funded openings were extracted from these pages.

### E. Identified research gaps and planned next searches

The researcher identified the following gaps after the completed searches:

1. The available papers did not yet constitute the required foundational source set.
2. The research still needed official/original sources covering:
   - Transformer architecture
   - Pretraining
   - Scaling
   - Post-training
   - Alignment
   - Retrieval
   - Efficient systems
   - Multimodal systems
   - Evaluation and safety
3. The search had not yet found or verified the requested systems-venue papers for topics such as FlashAttention, vLLM, Megatron-LM, or other efficient and scalable machine-learning systems.
4. Current labs and faculty remained underdeveloped, especially in Europe and Asia.
5. Current faculty affiliations needed verification to avoid stale recommendations.
6. Admissions, funding, and testing norms had not yet been researched.
7. The planned next actions were:
   - A narrow search for official European and Asian laboratory/faculty pages.
   - A search for official admissions, funding, and testing norms.
   - Verification of candidate paper and laboratory pages by opening them.

### F. Evidence and verification status

Every returned search result contained the instruction:

> “Open this URL with web_fetch before using it as evidence.”

No `web_fetch` calls were made in the available research record. Therefore:

- The URLs were discovered through search but were not opened.
- Paper abstracts, methods, findings, author lists, institutional affiliations, and publication metadata were not independently checked.
- Laboratory membership and faculty affiliations were not checked.
- No source update dates were extracted.
- The search results were accessed in the September 13, 2026 research context, but the underlying pages’ latest update dates remain unknown.
- The paper titles and venue/year cues above are only those shown by the search results.
- The discovered sources cannot yet support a rigorous substantive comparison of all requested research directions without further verification.

### G. Requested topics for which no substantive findings were gathered yet

The completed tool calls did **not** yet produce verified, detailed findings for:

- A decision framework tailored to the student’s unknown GPA, rank, university, coursework, research, publications, projects, English level, geographic preferences, budget, or other constraints.

No rigorous advisory conclusions about these subjects were present in the gathered tool output.

## **List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

### 1. United States search

**Tool:** `web_search`  
**Query:**  
> `site:cmu.edu machine learning PhD admissions funding stipend TOEFL application fee deadline site:stanford.edu CS PhD admissions funding deadline site:berkeley.edu EECS PhD admissions funding site:washington.edu CSE PhD admissions funding official`

**Search engine reported:** `ddgs_brave_fallback`  
**Results returned:** 10

The search identified official admissions, funding, and program pages for:

- Carnegie Mellon University’s Machine Learning Ph.D. program [1]
- Stanford Computer Science Ph.D. admissions [2]
- Carnegie Mellon School of Computer Science graduate admissions [3]
- Stanford Computer Science Ph.D. funding [4]
- Carnegie Mellon Computer Science doctoral admissions [5]
- Stanford Computer Science graduate application deadlines [6]
- UC Berkeley EECS graduate research-program admissions [7]
- Carnegie Mellon Machine Learning incoming Ph.D. student information [8]
- Carnegie Mellon’s prospective-student Machine Learning Ph.D. page [9]
- UC Berkeley EECS graduate-admissions FAQ [10]

**Researcher’s recorded assessment after this search:**

> “The first search identified authoritative US admissions and funding hubs for CMU, Stanford, and Berkeley, enough to establish the US model (bachelor-entry, structured coursework/quals, multiyear assistantship/fellowship). I still need official primary sources across Canada, UK/Europe, and Asia plus immigration/employment rules. Given the very broad request and five-search cap, the next searches should each cover regions with highly targeted institutional and government domains; individual pages can then be opened in parallel.”

No University of Washington page was returned despite its inclusion in the query.

---

### 2. Canada search

**Tool:** `web_search`  
**Query:**  
> `official PhD computer science admissions funding international Toronto UBC McGill Montreal Mila bachelor TOEFL deadline stipend Canada PGWP`

**Search engine reported:** `duckduckgo_html`  
**Results returned:** 10

The search returned official sources for:

- McGill doctoral funding opportunities [11]
- McGill’s Computer Science Ph.D. program [12]
- McGill School of Computer Science’s prospective graduate-student FAQ [13]
- UBC’s Ph.D. Applicants Hub [14]
- A second URL for McGill School of Computer Science’s graduate FAQ [17]
- McGill’s graduate admissions and application procedures [20]

The search also returned four non-primary commercial or advisory pages:

- Collegedunia’s overview of Ph.D. study in Canada [15]
- AcademicJobs’ guide to Canadian Ph.D. costs and funding [16]
- Collegedunia’s McGill Computer Science Ph.D. page [18]
- IRCCGuide’s overview of admissions at Toronto, McGill, and UBC [19]

These four pages were not accepted as authoritative evidence because the requested report called for primary and official sources.

**Researcher’s recorded assessment after this search:**

> “The Canadian search produced solid official McGill program/funding/admissions pages and UBC’s central PhD page, but missed Toronto and Montréal specifics and IRCC. McGill can anchor one representative conventional department while Toronto/Mila should be captured via later direct institutional URLs if found. Still missing nearly all non-North-American regions, so prioritize broad official-source searches for UK/Europe and Asia rather than over-search Canada.”

No official University of Toronto, Université de Montréal, Mila, or Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada page was returned.

---

### 3. United Kingdom search

**Tool:** `web_search`  
**Query:**  
> `official DPhil PhD computer science admissions funding fees stipend deadline Oxford Cambridge UCL Edinburgh international student UK graduate visa AI NLP`

**Search engine reported:** `duckduckgo_html`  
**Results returned:** 10

The search returned official pages for:

- Oxford’s DPhil in Computer Science [21]
- Oxford Computer Science research studentships and scholarships [22]
- Cambridge Computer Science Ph.D. admissions [23]
- A second Oxford Computer Science fees and funding URL [24]
- Oxford’s central graduate fees and funding information [25]
- UCL’s four-year Computer Science MPhil/Ph.D. program [26]
- Cambridge Computer Science funding information [27]
- Oxford Blavatnik School DPhil fees and funding [28]
- Cambridge’s central postgraduate funding information [30]

One non-primary commercial page was also returned:

- Collegedunia’s Oxford Computer Science doctorate page [29]

That page was not accepted as authoritative evidence because the requested report specified direct official sources.

**Researcher’s recorded assessment after this search:**

> “This gives high-quality official pages for Oxford, Cambridge and UCL, covering both traditional supervisor-led three-to-four-year UK doctorates and a four-year cohort model. Edinburgh did not surface, but these three are representative enough if supplemented by UKRI and government visa sources. Need continental employed/vacancy models and Asian destinations in the two remaining searches.”

No official University of Edinburgh, UK Research and Innovation, or United Kingdom government Graduate visa page was returned.

---

### 4. Planning/reflection tool calls

Three `think_tool` calls were made after the regional searches. Their complete substantive contents are reproduced above. They established the following research plan:

- Use CMU, Stanford, and Berkeley as authoritative United States anchors.
- Use McGill as a representative conventional Canadian computer-science department, while seeking Toronto/Mila and official Canadian immigration sources later.
- Use Oxford and Cambridge as representative traditional United Kingdom doctorates and UCL as a representative four-year cohort model.
- Prioritize official sources for continental Europe, Asia, immigration, and labor-market rules in later searches.
- Avoid over-reliance on non-primary commercial aggregators.

No further searches, page-fetch calls, or document-opening calls appear in the research record supplied here.

---

## **Fully Comprehensive Findings**

### A. Scope actually covered by the completed research

The completed searches found candidate official source hubs for parts of the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. They did **not** complete the requested global comparison.

The available record contains search-result titles and URLs, along with the researcher’s planning assessments. Every search result explicitly carried the instruction:

> “Open this URL with web_fetch before using it as evidence.”

No `web_fetch` calls are present in the supplied record. Therefore, the underlying pages were not opened, and no page text was extracted or verified. The source titles and URLs can be preserved as a research map, but they cannot support detailed claims about current eligibility, deadlines, funding, fees, language scores, curriculum, immigration rules, or employment outcomes.

No source access dates or page update dates were collected. The user’s requested reference date is September 13, 2026, but the currentness of the linked material was not verified.

---

### B. United States sources and preliminary institutional coverage

#### Carnegie Mellon University

The search identified several official Carnegie Mellon sources:

- The official “Ph.D. Program in Machine Learning” page [1]
- The School of Computer Science graduate-admissions page [3]
- The Computer Science Department’s doctoral-admissions page [5]
- The Machine Learning Department’s incoming Ph.D. student-information page [8]
- The Machine Learning Department’s prospective-student Ph.D. page [9]

These pages were identified as likely sources for program structure, doctoral admissions, incoming-student requirements, and Machine Learning Ph.D. information. However, none was opened, so no specific admission rule, deadline, fee, stipend, degree prerequisite, testing policy, curriculum requirement, qualifying examination, or funding guarantee was extracted.

The researcher’s preliminary assessment stated that the United States results were “enough to establish the US model (bachelor-entry, structured coursework/quals, multiyear assistantship/fellowship).” That statement was recorded as a planning assessment, not as a verified extraction from the pages.

#### Stanford University

The search identified official Stanford Computer Science pages for:

- Ph.D. admissions [2]
- Ph.D. funding [4]
- Graduate application deadlines [6]

These pages were intended to support Stanford-specific rules on admission, funding, and deadlines. No contents were fetched, so no exact deadlines, stipend amounts, fee figures, English-test requirements, Graduate Record Examination policy, or funding duration was preserved in the record.

#### University of California, Berkeley

The search identified official Berkeley EECS pages for:

- Graduate research-program admissions [7]
- Graduate-admissions frequently asked questions [10]

These pages were likely relevant to admission eligibility, application procedures, testing policies, and research-degree structure. No specific contents were opened or extracted.

#### University of Washington

Although University of Washington CSE was included in the search query, no Washington result was returned. Consequently, the available research contains no official Washington admissions, funding, curriculum, faculty, laboratory, or placement source.

---

### C. Canada sources and preliminary institutional coverage

#### McGill University

The search identified official McGill sources for:

- Doctoral student funding opportunities [11]
- The Computer Science Ph.D. program [12]
- The School of Computer Science’s graduate/prospective-student FAQ, available through two URLs [13][17]
- University-wide graduate admissions and application procedures [20]

These sources were intended to cover the Computer Science Ph.D., graduate admissions, eligibility, application procedures, and doctoral funding. Because the pages were not opened, no exact McGill requirement or amount was extracted.

The two McGill FAQ URLs may refer to the same or substantially similar resource, but both distinct URLs were returned and are retained in the source record [13][17].

The researcher’s assessment was:

> “The Canadian search produced solid official McGill program/funding/admissions pages and UBC’s central PhD page, but missed Toronto and Montréal specifics and IRCC. McGill can anchor one representative conventional department while Toronto/Mila should be captured via later direct institutional URLs if found.”

Thus, McGill was selected provisionally as a representative conventional Canadian computer-science department, but no detailed comparison was completed.

#### University of British Columbia

The search returned UBC’s official “PhD Applicants Hub” [14]. This is a central university source rather than a specifically identified Computer Science Ph.D. page. No program-specific UBC Computer Science admissions, funding, faculty, laboratory, or curriculum source was gathered.

#### University of Toronto, Université de Montréal, and Mila

The search query included Toronto, Montréal, and Mila, but no official page from these institutions was returned. Therefore, the record contains no verified source for:

- University of Toronto Computer Science or related AI doctoral admissions
- Université de Montréal Computer Science doctoral admissions
- Mila-affiliated doctoral pathways, faculty matching, funding, or application arrangements

#### Canadian immigration and post-study work

The query included “Canada PGWP,” but no official Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada source was returned. A private site named IRCCGuide appeared [19], but it is not the official Canadian government immigration department and was not accepted as primary evidence.

Consequently, the research did not establish official rules for:

- Post-Graduation Work Permit eligibility or duration
- Study-permit requirements
- Work authorization during study
- Permanent-residence pathways
- Any China-specific Canadian immigration issue

#### Non-primary Canadian results

Four non-primary sources appeared:

- “PhD in Canada 2027: Top Universities, Fees, Requirements and Scholarships,” Collegedunia [15]
- “PhD Cost Canada 2026: Tuition & Funding Guide,” AcademicJobs [16]
- “Ph.D Computer Science at McGill University [MCGILL], Montreal Fees …,” Collegedunia [18]
- “2026 Top 3 Canadian University Admission Requirements: UofT, McGill, UBC,” IRCCGuide [19]

No information from these sources was incorporated because the assignment required primary university and government sources.

---

### D. United Kingdom sources and preliminary institutional coverage

#### University of Oxford

The search identified official Oxford sources for:

- The DPhil in Computer Science [21]
- Computer Science research studentships and scholarships [22]
- A second Department of Computer Science fees/funding URL [24]
- Central graduate fees and funding [25]
- Blavatnik School of Government DPhil fees and funding [28]

The Computer Science sources were likely intended to support Oxford-specific admissions, fees, funding, duration, and application information. The central graduate page was likely intended to support university-wide funding and fee rules. The Blavatnik School page concerns a different academic unit and would not directly establish Computer Science DPhil rules; it may only have been potentially useful for broader Oxford DPhil funding context.

The two Computer Science fees URLs have different paths—one ends in `fees.html`, while the other ends in `fees`—and were returned separately [22][24]. Both are retained.

No pages were opened, so no exact Oxford requirements, English-test thresholds, application deadlines, fee figures, living-cost estimates, stipend values, scholarship deadlines, proposal rules, or faculty-contact expectations were extracted.

#### University of Cambridge

The search identified official Cambridge sources for:

- Department of Computer Science and Technology Ph.D. admissions [23]
- Departmental funding information [27]
- Central postgraduate funding information [30]

These pages were intended to support Cambridge admissions and funding analysis. No page content was fetched, and no exact eligibility rule, degree expectation, deadline, fee, stipend, English threshold, or supervisor-contact process was extracted.

#### University College London

The search identified UCL’s official “Computer Science (4 Year Programme) MPhil/PhD” page [26].

The researcher treated this as a representative “four-year cohort model,” in contrast with “traditional supervisor-led three-to-four-year UK doctorates” at Oxford and Cambridge. This was a preliminary characterization made from the result context; the page itself was not fetched.

No exact UCL entry requirements, program curriculum, rotations, cohort structure, funding package, tuition, application fee, deadline, or English-language rules were extracted.

#### University of Edinburgh

The search query included Edinburgh, but no official Edinburgh source surfaced. The researcher explicitly recorded:

> “Edinburgh did not surface.”

Therefore, no Edinburgh doctoral program, Centre for Doctoral Training, NLP group, funding, or admissions evidence was collected.

#### United Kingdom funding and immigration

The researcher noted that Oxford, Cambridge, and UCL should be “supplemented by UKRI and government visa sources.” No official UK Research and Innovation or UK government immigration source was ultimately gathered.

Consequently, the research did not verify:

- UKRI doctoral stipend levels
- International fee coverage
- Doctoral Training Partnership or Centre for Doctoral Training funding eligibility
- Student visa conditions
- Graduate visa duration and eligibility
- Skilled Worker or Global Talent routes
- Employment restrictions during doctoral study

#### Non-primary United Kingdom result

One commercial source appeared:

- “University of Oxford DPhil Computer Science 2026: Admission, Fees …,” Collegedunia [29]

It was not used as evidence because the requested research required official university and government sources.

---

### E. Regions and subjects not researched in the supplied record

Despite the initial plan to conduct additional searches, no completed searches or source collection are present for the following requested destinations:

- Switzerland:
  - ETH Zurich
  - EPFL

  - Max Planck institutes

No government labor, post-study work, or immigration sources were gathered for the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, continental Europe, Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, or South Korea.

---

### F. Requested comparison dimensions for which no verified data was extracted

Because no result pages were fetched, the research record does not contain verified program-level data for the following requested dimensions:

- Direct bachelor-to-doctorate availability
- Whether a master’s is expected or formally required
- Treatment of Chinese bachelor’s or master’s credentials
- Minimum grade-point average, class rank, or degree classification
- Required mathematical or computer-science preparation
- Structured or cohort doctoral training

- Curriculum requirements

- Expected or maximum doctoral duration
- Supervision and committee models
- Compute facilities, data resources, or interdisciplinary AI centers
- Publication culture
- Industry partnerships

- Local AI labor-market prospects

- A dated exchange-rate assumption

No exact 2027–2028 dates or financial amounts were found or verified. Accordingly, the required warning remains applicable: exact 2027–2028 dates and amounts may not yet be published and must be checked against live official pages when available.

---

### G. Limits of the available findings

The search results repeatedly instructed that each URL had to be opened with `web_fetch` before it could be used as evidence. Since no page was opened:

1. Source titles and URLs are the only direct source data preserved.
2. The researcher’s regional-model statements are preliminary planning judgments.
3. No detailed admissions, funding, curriculum, faculty, immigration, or employment claim should be treated as verified from these searches alone.
4. No source access date or page update date is available.
5. No exchange-rate conversion was performed.
6. No applicant-specific portfolio or tiering framework was produced.
7. No assessment could be tailored to the applicant because the record contains no exact grade-point average, rank, institution, coursework, research, publications, software projects, English level, destination preferences, finances, or personal constraints.

---

## **List of All Relevant Sources (with citations in the report)**

### Sources

args.reflection: The two parallel agents produced an uneven but usable research map. The program agent found official admissions/funding hubs for representative United States, Canadian, and United Kingdom programs, while the technical agent found primary proceedings papers and official United States NLP lab pages. However, both explicitly failed to fetch and verify page contents, and continental Europe and Asia are largely absent. Because the hard limit allows at most two ConductResearch calls total and both have now been used, I cannot delegate further. A separate final-report agent can synthesize cautiously from the collected source map and general comparative structure, clearly labeling unverified or estimated details, omitting false precision, warning that 2027–2028 dates and amounts require live rechecking, and using representative program-group descriptions rather than pretending comprehensive verified figures. The findings are sufficient to indicate research completion under the imposed budget, but the final report must be transparent about the evidence gaps.

research_brief: As of September 13, 2026, which artificial-intelligence PhD research directions and programs abroad would best fit me over a roughly 1–2-year application horizon, given that I am a Computer Science and Technology undergraduate at a prestigious university in Jiangsu, have excellent academic performance and two consecutive years of university scholarships, and am primarily interested in natural language processing and deep learning—especially applied, implementation-heavy research, experimental engineering, and AI system building—with the long-term goal of industrial R&D while retaining strong academic-research and general employability options? Compare major destinations in North America, Europe, and Asia, including differences between direct-entry PhDs from a bachelor’s degree, programs that expect or require a master’s, structured doctoral programs, and professor- or project-based positions. First, identify and compare promising NLP/deep-learning subfields—such as language-model training and adaptation, efficient and scalable ML systems, retrieval and knowledge-intensive NLP, multimodal language systems, evaluation and reliability, human-centered or domain-applied NLP, and other relevant emerging directions—without assuming that I am committed to any narrower topic; assess each direction’s research maturity, prerequisite knowledge, implementation intensity, publication opportunities, compute and data requirements, fit with industrial R&D, likely durability beyond current trends, and representative laboratories, faculty, papers, and employers. Then compare representative universities and programs across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, continental Europe, Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, and other justified destinations, evaluating faculty and laboratory fit, recent research strengths and output, curriculum and qualifying-exam structure, degree duration, supervision model, access to compute/data and interdisciplinary centers, industry collaborations and internships, publication culture, alumni placement, local AI employment prospects, post-study work or immigration considerations, and practical risks such as dependence on a single supervisor or grant. For each representative program, summarize official eligibility and application requirements for an international applicant educated in China, including whether direct bachelor-to-PhD admission is possible, expected academic and mathematical/CS preparation, English-language tests and waiver rules, GRE or other testing policies, research-proposal requirements, faculty-contact norms, deadlines for likely 2027 and 2028 entry cycles where published, application fees, tuition, mandatory charges, estimated living costs, stipend levels, funding duration, teaching or research obligations, scholarship mechanisms, and whether funding is guaranteed, competitive, supervisor-dependent, or insufficient for normal living expenses. Clearly distinguish official facts from estimates and compare costs in local currency plus a common reference currency when feasible. Produce a region-by-region comparison and a provisional reach/match/safer shortlist or tiering methodology, while explicitly noting that my exact GPA, class rank, university name, core mathematics and CS coursework, research experience, publications, major AI/software projects, English proficiency, preferred countries, budget, and personal constraints have not been specified; do not invent these facts, and explain how different values would change the recommendations. Include a diagnostic checklist for those missing details and identify the highest-priority readiness gaps likely to matter for NLP/deep-learning PhD admission. Finally, create two concrete preparation pathways—an accelerated approximately 12-month route and a stronger approximately 18–24-month route—with month- or quarter-level milestones for auditing prerequisites in linear algebra, calculus, probability/statistics, optimization, algorithms, systems, machine learning, deep learning, and NLP; reproducing influential papers; building technically substantial and reproducible GitHub projects; obtaining research-assistant experience and mentorship; choosing feasible research questions; conducting experiments and writing a paper or technical report; targeting suitable conferences, workshops, or preprints without encouraging low-quality publication; pursuing relevant industrial or research internships; preparing English tests and any required standardized tests; developing a faculty/program tracking system; contacting potential supervisors appropriately; securing strong recommendation letters; drafting the CV, statement of purpose, research statement/proposal, and writing sample; selecting balanced application portfolios; and managing deadlines, interviews, offers, funding comparisons, and contingencies such as applying first to a research-oriented master’s or full-time research-assistant position. Prioritize primary and current sources: official university, department, graduate-school, funding, immigration, and faculty/laboratory pages; original papers and official proceedings from venues such as ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, and relevant systems conferences; and official employer or government labor information. Link directly to those sources, state the access or update date, flag information that may change by the application cycle, and use secondary rankings or blogs only as clearly labeled supplementary context rather than decisive evidence.
